training-data.t: A spam classifier is fitted to a set of **training emails**. Its parameters are tuned to these particular examples.

high-training-score.t: Scored on those same emails, it reaches **98 percent accuracy**. That looks excellent, but the model **has already seen these emails**.

new-data.t: Now fresh emails arrive that were **not used to fit** the model. This **validation data** shows how the model behaves on mail it has never seen.

performance-drop.t: Validation accuracy is only **84 percent**, a **14-point gap**. The validation score is the better guide to real use. A large gap is the overfitting you met in Regression in Practice.

imbalanced-data.t: A mailbox of 100 emails has **95 legitimate and only 5 spam**. When one class is rare, **accuracy can hide a lot**.

always-negative.h: A MODEL THAT ALWAYS SAYS LEGITIMATE
always-negative.t: Consider a lazy model that predicts **legitimate for every email**. It never flags anything.

high-accuracy.t: It is right for all 95 legitimate emails: **95 correct out of 100**, so 95 percent accuracy. That sounds great.

missed-positive-class.t: Yet it catches **0 of the 5 spam** emails. The high accuracy came from **ignoring the rare class** completely.

need-better-metrics.t: Accuracy is **one metric, not the whole story**. Next comes a table of the four outcomes, then precision, recall and F1, which look at **each kind of mistake**.
